name: FPGA-NFC
firmware_note: The Verilog is the entire product - there is no separate firmware/hardware split. It targets any FPGA (Altera Cyclone IV by default for the 81.36MHz PLL primitive; other vendors need a substitute clock IP).
price_note: No product exists to buy - $20 is a rough BOM estimate for the NFC_BreakoutBoard (AD7276B ADC, FDV301N MOSFET, coil, passives) via the linked OSHWHub gerbers, and does not include the FPGA dev board itself (any board with a spare clock, 4 GPIO and a UART bridge works; a cheap Cyclone IV board runs $15-40 more).
skill_note: You are writing and debugging the ISO14443A PHY and MAC layers yourself in Verilog, then soldering an analogue front end and tuning a 4-turn antenna coil by hand. This is an RF and digital-logic project, not a 'buy and flash' tool.
build_note: Fabricate the NFC_BreakoutBoard PCB from the provided gerbers, hand-solder the AD7276B ADC and analogue front end, wire it to any FPGA dev board's GPIO (ADC_SCK runs at up to 40.68MHz, so the README explicitly warns against Dupont jumper wires), then synthesize and load the Verilog.
summary: A from-scratch ISO14443A card reader built entirely in FPGA logic and a handful of discrete parts (a 3Msps AD7276B ADC, an FDV301N MOSFET, a diode envelope detector and a 4-turn coil) instead of a dedicated NFC chip like the PN532 or ST25R3916. It talks to a host PC over a plain 9600-baud serial line and has been demonstrated reading MIFARE Classic (M1) cards. It's a teaching/hobby project by a single developer, not a product.
honest_take: This does exactly one useful thing that a $9 PN532 breakout doesn't: it proves the NFC PHY layer isn't magic - carrier generation, ASK demodulation via envelope detection, and the ISO14443A frame format are all implemented in visible, readable Verilog. But as a tool it is strictly worse than a PN532 or Proxmark3 for any practical RFID work: no write support beyond the protocol layer, no anti-collision beyond basic REQA/ANTICOLL, no MIFARE Classic crypto attacks, and a carrier that auto-shuts-off after 1.2 seconds of serial inactivity. Buy this only if the point is learning FPGA-based RF signal processing; buy a PN532 if the point is reading cards.
best_for: Learning how ISO14443A's ASK envelope detection and framing actually work at the signal level
FPGA/Verilog practice with a real RF front end
Demonstrating that dedicated NFC silicon isn't required for basic 13.56MHz reading
not_for: Anyone who just wants to read/clone/emulate NFC cards - buy a PN532 or Proxmark3 instead
MIFARE Classic key-recovery attacks (nested/darkside/hardnested) - not implemented
Any use requiring tag emulation - this project only implements the PCD (reader) role

hardware.mcu_primary_note: No MCU. Protocol logic, DSP, and UART framing all run as Verilog RTL inside the FPGA fabric (any FPGA large enough for a small UART+DSP design; author used an Altera Cyclone IV).

radios.note: 3Msps 12-bit SPI ADC (confirmed against the Analog Devices datasheet), used to sample the 847.5kHz subcarrier envelope from the PICC-to-PCD response, not the 13.56MHz carrier directly.

hardware.battery_note: None. Powered from the FPGA board's USB/external supply plus a separate 7-9V rail for the antenna drive circuit (J1 on the breakout board).
hardware.storage: None - all logic is synthesized into FPGA fabric, no persistent storage
connectivity: UART (via the FPGA board's own USB-UART bridge, e.g. FT232/CP2102/CH340)
hardware.gpio: 4 FPGA GPIO pins used: ADC_CSN, ADC_SCLK, ADC_SDATA, CARRIER_OUT, at 3.3V or 2.5V logic
notable_physical: 4-turn hand-wound antenna coil on the breakout PCB
Separate 7-9V supply input for the carrier drive MOSFET
Onboard status LEDs for PLL lock, carrier-on, and RX-complete

hf_1356_read.note: Full ISO14443A PHY/MAC in Verilog; demonstrated reading MIFARE Classic (M1) cards including door-control cards and blank white cards.

hf_1356_write.note: README states the protocol layer supports send/receive framing, but no ready-made write/format application is provided - you'd write the M1 write commands yourself over serial.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Only implements the PCD (reader) role, not PICC (card) emulation.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: No key-recovery or crypto attacks implemented - this is a bare reader, not a Proxmark-style attack tool.

mifare_desfire.note: No DESFire (ISO14443-4/T=CL) support - the frame handler only implements the plain ISO14443A/MIFARE Classic path described in the README.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: No NDEF/Type 4 application layer implemented - only raw ISO14443A frame send/receive over serial.

emv_read.note: No ISO14443-4/APDU layer, which EMV contactless requires - not implemented.

iso15693.note: README says the analogue hardware supports ISO15693, but the Verilog protocol layer for it was never written ('I haven't write its protocol in FPGA').

felica.note: Not implemented - project is ISO14443A-only at the protocol level.

magspoof.note: No magnetic-stripe hardware - this is a 13.56MHz reader only.

nfc_relay.note: Single-sided reader design; no second PICC-emulation stage exists to relay a session.

lf_125khz_read.note: No 125kHz front end at all - hardware is tuned exclusively for the 13.56MHz HF band.

scriptable.note: Plain-text hex-over-serial protocol at 9600 baud, one command/response per line - trivial to script from any language.

standalone_untethered.note: Requires a host PC sending serial commands; the FPGA auto-cuts the carrier 1.2s after the last command with nothing to reissue it.

web_ui.note: Serial terminal only ('Serial Assistant' recommended over Putty); no web or GUI interface shipped.

app_store.note: Single-developer Verilog repo; no companion app ecosystem.

sd_logging.note: No storage of any kind on the board - all captured data goes out over the live serial link.

legal.notes: A bare-metal 13.56MHz reader you build and program yourself. Owning and reading cards you're authorized to read (your own access cards, your own tags) is not restricted in most jurisdictions. Reading or cloning someone else's access credentials without authorization is a separate legal question wherever you are - check local law before pointing it at a card that isn't yours.

name: RFID HF Repeater Large
price_note: $20.00 at Hacker Warehouse (SKU MWG-V3L). A competing passive booster of the same kind (Lab401's 62mm 'large' range booster) sells for EUR22 (~$24); Midwest Gadgets also sells smaller 28mm versions in 4-packs on Tindie for less per unit, so $20 for a large single card is in line with the rest of the category rather than an outlier.
skill_note: It's a passive card-sized resonator - place it between the obstruction and the reader. No configuration, no firmware, no electronics knowledge needed.
build_note: Fully passive, ready to use out of the box - nothing to assemble or program.
summary: A passive, unpowered 13.56MHz resonant coil in a 3x3 inch card, sold to relay a reader's HF field through an obstruction (a wallet, a bag, a thin door panel) and recover a few millimeters of lost read range. Hacker Warehouse's own listing quotes an example gain of 5-9mm of extra read distance; a same-technology competing product (Lab401's range booster line) claims up to double the read range on cards/fobs, which gives a sense of how wide the real-world variance is depending on target tag size and reader geometry.
honest_take: This is a tuned LC resonator, not an amplifier - it has no battery and no active gain stage, so it cannot make a card readable from meters away or defeat a Faraday-shielded wallet; it only recovers some of the range an obstruction otherwise costs you, and how much (Hacker Warehouse quotes single-digit millimeters, a competing seller quotes up to 2x) depends entirely on how well its resonant frequency and coupling geometry happen to match your reader and card. For genuine long-range HF field manipulation (the kind used in real relay/ghost-and-leech attacks) you want an active repeater built from two coupled reader/emulator stages with real amplification, not a passive card like this one.
best_for: Recovering a few mm of NFC/RFID read range lost to a phone case, wallet or thin door panel
Physical pentest kits where a slightly thicker badge holder is defeating quick taps
not_for: Long-range relay attacks (meters, not millimeters) - needs an active two-stage repeater, not a passive card
Defeating RFID-blocking (Faraday) wallets or sleeves - a passive resonator cannot punch through shielding

name: Mellon
firmware_note: A Python proof-of-concept toolkit, not firmware for a fixed device - it runs on a laptop and drives generic USB-to-RS485 adapters.
price_note: The code is free; $15 is a rough estimate for one generic USB-to-RS485 adapter. A full active man-in-the-middle setup needs three adapters per the README (roughly $30-45 total) plus a breadboard, not counting the laptop you run the Python on.
skill_note: You need to understand OSDP wiring (RS485 A/B, controller vs. reader roles), physically tap or insert into the wiring between a door controller and a reader, and interpret raw protocol captures - this is not a point-and-click tool.
build_note: No enclosure or kit - wire up to three USB-to-RS485 adapters on a breadboard per Bishop Fox's own setup and run the Python scripts (attack_osdp.py) against the physical RS485 bus, or against the included vulnserver.py to practice without hardware.
summary: Bishop Fox's reference proof-of-concept toolkit for attacking OSDP (Open Supervised Device Protocol), the RS485 protocol that connects most modern access-control card readers to their door controllers. It implements the five attacks from their 2023 Black Hat/DEF CON research 'Badge of Shame': passive eavesdropping of unencrypted card numbers, forcing an encryption downgrade, extracting the shared key during install mode, capturing keys sent during a key-rotation, and brute-forcing weak/default keys. It's a research tool released alongside the talk, not a commercial product, and it deliberately does not read or clone RFID/NFC cards itself - it attacks the wire between the reader and the controller.
honest_take: Mellon is the reference implementation behind real, disclosed OSDP weaknesses - not marketing. The catch is that most of its attacks (downgrade, install-mode key extraction, weak-key brute force) require physical access to the RS485 wire between reader and controller, which usually means opening a reader or getting inside a wiring closet; this is a wired-access-control research tool, not a wireless card-cloning tool like a Proxmark or Flipper - it has zero RFID/NFC card-reading capability of its own, which is easy to assume given the category it's filed under. Independent commentary (IPVM) has since pushed back that the practical exploitation bar is higher than the DEF CON framing implied, since several attacks need sustained physical bus access most attackers won't have. The single most common misconception is treating this as a plug-and-play badge cloner - it attacks the wire, not the card.
best_for: Physical penetration testers validating whether a client's OSDP install actually uses Secure Channel encryption
Learning OSDP's actual wire-level weaknesses from the tool that demonstrated them
Practicing against the bundled vulnserver.py without needing real access-control hardware
not_for: Wireless/contactless card cloning - this attacks the RS485 wire between reader and controller, not the card-to-reader RF link, and has no NFC/RFID read capability at all
Anyone without RS485/OSDP wiring knowledge or physical access to the reader-controller cable

hf_1356_read.note: Despite being filed under RFID/NFC (the closest existing category), Mellon has no card-reading hardware or code at all - it attacks the OSDP wire between an existing reader and controller, not the card itself.

lf_125khz_read.note: No LF hardware or code - not applicable to a wire-protocol attack tool.

name: RFIDetector
price_note: No retail listing exists anywhere - $15 is an unverified low estimate for a credit-card-sized PCB with two coils, a handful of Schottky diodes and LEDs. Treat this figure as a guess, not a sourced price.
skill_note: Small SMD passive/diode design - buildable by anyone comfortable hand-soldering fine-pitch parts, but you're fabricating the PCB yourself from KiCad files with no vendor to buy it assembled.
build_note: CERN-OHL-S licensed KiCad hardware (schematic + PCB, revision history rev0.1 through rev0.22) with no assembled option - order the boards yourself and hand-solder the parts.
summary: A small open-hardware PCB (CERN-OHL-S licensed) that indicates whether it is sitting in an active LF (125kHz) or HF (13.56MHz) RFID reader field. Direct inspection of the rev0.22 KiCad schematic shows it is a purely passive/analogue design - two tuned coils, nine 1N5819WS Schottky diodes for envelope detection on each band, and three status LEDs, with solder-jumper pads to select modes - not a microcontroller-based device.
honest_take: This is a passive field-presence indicator, not a reader or a security scanner: it tells you 'something nearby is generating an LF or HF field,' not what protocol, what data, or whose reader it is. It has no microcontroller, no logging, and no way to distinguish a legitimate access-control reader from a skimmer or from your own Flipper Zero sitting in your pocket. With 3 GitHub stars and a single contributor it is effectively a personal project shared as open hardware, not a maintained product - expect to debug your own PCB order.

name: simple_rfid
firmware_note: Arduino sketch is the entire firmware; no alternate builds exist.
price_note: Rough BOM estimate: an Arduino Nano clone (~$3-5) plus an RDM6300 125kHz reader module (~$3-5). PCB manufacturing through the linked PCBWay project adds a few dollars per board in small quantities on top of that.
skill_note: Off-the-shelf Arduino Nano + RDM6300 module wired per the schematic and flashed with the provided sketch - straightforward for anyone who has done basic Arduino projects, no RF design of your own required.
build_note: Schematic and PCB layout provided (with a PCBWay fabrication link); solder the Nano and RDM6300 module to the board and flash the Arduino sketch from the firmware folder.
summary: A DIY 125kHz LF RFID reader/cloner/emulator built from an Arduino Nano and an off-the-shelf RDM6300 reader module, with open schematic, PCB layout and firmware. It targets the same basic EM4100/T5577-class tags as any generic 125kHz copier - the RDM6300 module does the actual RF demodulation, the Arduino handles UID capture, storage and re-transmission.
honest_take: The README describes this in one line as an 'emulator/cloner/reader' with no further technical detail on how writing or emulation is actually implemented - and that claim deserves real skepticism, because the RDM6300's own datasheet documents it purely as a 125kHz receive module (UART UID output only), not a writer. Genuine T5577 rewriting normally needs either a stronger dedicated write driver or a documented trick to repurpose the RDM6300's own coil in reverse, and this project's one-paragraph README doesn't say which it uses. The chip underneath is the same cheap part found in countless sub-$10 generic 125kHz copier kits already on the market - this project's real value is that it's open source and buildable from raw parts, not that it does anything those kits don't. It only covers 125kHz LF (EM4100/T5577-class) tags - it has no HF/13.56MHz capability at all, so it can't touch MIFARE or any modern access card.

name: HiLetgo PN532 NFC RFID Module Kit
price_note: $8.99 is a representative Amazon marketplace price for a PN532 breakout of this class; HiLetgo and near-identical clone boards from other brands (Elechouse, generic) commonly sell in the $8-15 range depending on antenna size and included accessories.
skill_note: A bare breakout board - you wire it to a microcontroller or SBC over I2C/SPI/UART and run libnfc or a vendor SDK yourself; no standalone app.
build_note: No soldering typically required beyond header pins (often pre-soldered); wire to a Raspberry Pi, Arduino or similar host and install libnfc or an equivalent driver.
summary: A breakout board for NXP's PN532, the NFC controller chip found in the overwhelming majority of phones and consumer NFC readers, exposing I2C, SPI and UART (HSU) interfaces. It reads and writes NFC Type 1-4 tags and MIFARE Classic/Ultralight, and can do ISO18092 peer-to-peer and limited card emulation - it is the standard low-cost building block behind countless libnfc, Arduino and Raspberry Pi RFID projects.
honest_take: This is genuinely the same silicon inside a large share of commercial NFC readers, not a toy chip - the PN532's read/write/P2P feature set is real, and NXP's own PN532 User Manual (UM0701-02) confirms full FeliCa support. But three things are commonly assumed and wrong: it does not do ISO15693 (a different chip family, e.g. ST25R3916, handles that); its 'card emulation' mode does not implement the MIFARE Classic authentication sequence as a target, so it can present static data but not fully impersonate an authenticating card; and DESFire (7-byte UID) detection is inconsistent across PN532 board variants - libnfc bug reports show Adafruit's version reliably sees DESFire/Ultralight/Jewel tags while cheaper Elechouse-style clones (which HiLetgo's board resembles) often see only 4-byte-UID MIFARE Classic cards. If you want a point-and-use device rather than a module to wire up yourself, a Flipper Zero or ACR122U is the better buy; if you're building your own project on a Pi or microcontroller, this is the standard part to reach for, just budget time for clone-board quirks.

summary: A self-contained hardware-pentest lab-in-a-box from Mindstorm Security: an Orange Pi Zero3 (Cortex-A53, 1.5GHz, 4GB RAM) single-board Linux computer with a touchscreen, running a Dockerized web interface in kiosk mode, bundled with a full physical toolkit (PCBite probes, eMMC reader, SOP flash sockets, SPI clips) for connecting to and dumping firmware from UART, SPI, JTAG, I2C and SWD interfaces on unknown target boards. honest_take: Two things to know before paying $11k. First, this is priced and positioned as a subscription service wrapped around hardware, not a one-time tool purchase - the headline price buys you a year of engineering support, hardware replacement and a cloud analysis pipeline, and it's unclear what the device is worth once that year lapses without renewing. name: ChipSHOVER
firmware_note: Marlin2-based stepper-control firmware, open source; the same repo also documents a lower-precision DIY build path NewAE chose not to sell as a product.
price_note: $10,000 direct from NewAE for the assembled 'PS1' kit (medium-resolution stage + ChipShover-One controller + power supply + accessories), quoted with a 2-week lead time. NewAE's own open-source repo documents a much cheaper low-resolution DIY path: a ~$500 off-the-shelf CNC frame plus an ~$180 open-source Archim2 controller board (~$680 total), which NewAE explicitly says it does not sell as a product because the precision/cost tradeoff isn't 'worth carrying' for them.
skill_note: A precision robotics platform for automated EM fault-injection mapping across a die surface - assumes you already understand fault injection and side-channel methodology; the ChipSHOVER only automates the physical positioning.
build_note: Ships assembled as the PS1 kit; controlled via onboard LCD for manual jogging or a Python API for scripted scans. NewAE's GitHub repo also documents a self-build low-resolution alternative for those willing to assemble a CNC frame and a $180 Archim2 controller themselves.
summary: A motorized 3-axis XYZ positioning stage from NewAE built to automate scanning an EM fault-injection probe or side-channel sensor across a chip's surface - something normally done by hand with a manual micromanipulator. The commercial PS1 kit uses a medium-resolution stage (156.25nm step size, ~3um backlash/repeatability) with NewAE's own ChipShover-One controller board; the open-source ChipShover GitHub repo also documents a cheaper, lower-precision DIY variant (781.25nm step, 50-100um backlash) built around a widely-available ~$500 CNC frame and an open ~$180 Archim2 controller, which NewAE deliberately doesn't sell as a finished product. It includes a direct mounting adapter for NewAE's own ChipSHOUTER EM fault-injection tool, and is controlled either from its onboard LCD or scripted over USB via Python.
honest_take: Despite the name similarity to the ChipSHOUTER, this is a completely different product - the ChipSHOUTER is the EM pulse generator itself, the ChipSHOVER is the robot arm that moves it (or any other probe) around a chip automatically. It does not inject faults or do side-channel capture on its own; you still need a ChipSHOUTER, an EM probe, or other sensing hardware to actually do the work, this just automates the tedious manual XY-scanning that fault-injection research otherwise requires. The bigger finding: NewAE open-sourced the whole design, including a DIY low-resolution build path (a common CNC frame plus an ~$180 open controller, roughly $680 all-in) that they explicitly chose not to productize because the precision is ~5x worse (781nm vs 156nm steps) and backlash is far higher (50-100um vs 3um). If your fault-injection work can tolerate that lower precision, building the DIY variant from NewAE's own open repo saves roughly $9,300 over the $10k PS1 kit - a genuinely rare case of a vendor publishing the cheap path around their own flagship product.

skill_note: A full SoC/crypto-core emulation target board for side-channel and fault-injection research on large security designs (e.g. OpenTitan) - this is research-lab-tier equipment, not a beginner side-channel board.

name: PhyWhisperer-USB (CW610)
price_note: $360 direct from NewAE; Crowd Supply lists the same board at $365.
skill_note: An in-line USB protocol monitor/trigger for timing side-channel and fault-injection captures against USB targets - assumes familiarity with USB 2.0 protocol framing and with ChipWhisperer-style capture workflows.
build_note: Ships assembled; sits in-line on the USB cable between host and target, controlled from Python.
summary: An in-line USB 2.0 Low/Full/High-Speed monitor and pattern trigger built around a Xilinx Spartan-7 XC7S15 FPGA and an Atmel/Microchip ATSAM3U (Cortex-M3) microcontroller. It buffers 8,192 bytes of captured USB traffic in FPGA block RAM, fires a cycle-accurate trigger when 1-64 bytes of masked pattern match (with 0-1,048,576 cycle programmable delay), includes a bypassable 5-ohm power shunt for correlating captures with power draw on an external scope, and feeds synchronized clock/trigger signals to ChipWhisperer capture hardware for USB-target power analysis and fault injection.
honest_take: This is a precision timing/triggering instrument, not a USB sniffer for casual protocol analysis - Wireshark with a USB capture driver, or a cheap USB protocol analyzer, does general-purpose USB traffic inspection far more conveniently. PhyWhisperer-USB earns its keep specifically for side-channel and fault-injection work against USB-connected targets, where you need a trigger that fires on exact protocol bytes with cycle-accurate timing synced to a ChipWhisperer - a niche need, but one nothing else in this price range addresses.

The differential and H-field probes measure power draw and EM emissions, which only becomes a side-channel attack once fed into capture and analysis software (ChipWhisperer or your own scope + DPA/CPA toolchain) and correlated against known plaintext/ciphertext. summary: NewAE's standard baseboard, released in 2016, for building ChipWhisperer side-channel and glitching target ('victim') boards. It supplies clean, filtered power at 1.2V/1.8V/2.5V/3.3V and an adjustable 1.25-3.5V rail, a crystal-socket oscillator, an onboard LC low-pass filter for accurate shunt-based power measurement, and diode-protected I/O for voltage glitch injection - all shared infrastructure so a target daughtercard only needs to carry the chip under test. NewAE's own documentation notes the daughtercards deliberately omit decoupling capacitors the chip vendor would normally include, specifically to keep power traces clean for measurement.
honest_take: This is the unglamorous infrastructure board that makes ChipWhisperer side-channel work reproducible across different target chips - it does nothing attack-related by itself, it just standardizes power filtering, clocking and glitch-injection wiring so daughtercards (STM32F3, XMEGA, AVR, FPGA targets) can be swapped without re-engineering the measurement setup each time. It's the right board to own once you're doing serious ChipWhisperer work across multiple target chip families; if you only ever plan to attack one specific chip, a purpose-built single-target board is cheaper.
